title: How Much You Should Save Before Buying Your First Investment Property
description: Calculating the capital requirements for becoming a landlord.
content:
Buying a rental property is different from buying a home to live in. Banks view it as a business transaction with higher risk. Consequently, the 'Cash to Close' requirements are significantly higher. You cannot use low-down-payment programs (like 3% Conventional) for pure investment properties. You need 20-25% down, closing costs, and substantial liquid reserves. Under-capitalization is the #1 reason new investors fail. This guide calculates the safe entry price for real estate investing.

Key Takeaways

  • The 25% Standard: Expect to put 25% down to get the best interest rate on a Single Family Rental. On a $200k house, that is $50k cash.
  • The Reserve Rule: Lenders require you to have 6 months of mortgage payments (PITI) in liquid cash after you buy. You cannot end with $0 in the bank.
  • The 'Capex' Fund: You need an immediate repair fund ($5k) for things that break in Month 1. Do not rely on cash flow to fix the roof.
  • House Hacking Exception: If you live in one unit of a multi-family (2-4 units), you can use an FHA loan with 3.5% down. This is the only way to bypass the high capital requirement.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Interest rates for investment properties are typically 0.5% - 1.0% higher than primary residence rates. You need a larger down payment to ensure the property 'Cash Flows' (Rent > Mortgage + Expenses) at these higher rates.

The Investor's Balance Sheet

Target Property: $300,000 Duplex (Investment Loan).

1. Acquisition Cash

  • Down Payment (25%): $75,000.
  • Closing Costs (4%): $12,000 (Higher points/fees).
  • Inspection/Appraisal: $1,000.
  • Total Upfront: $88,000.

2. Safety Reserves

  • Bank Requirement (6mo PITI): ~$10,000.
  • Maintenance Reserve: $5,000.
  • Vacancy Buffer: $2,000.
  • Total Reserves: $17,000.

Total 'Go' Number: $105,000.
Reality: If you have $50k, you aren't ready for a pure investment deal yet. Look at House Hacking or REITs.

How to Save for It

  1. Separate 'Real Estate' Fund: Keep this cash in T-Bills or a Money Market Fund. You need it liquid and safe. Don't risk it in stocks.
  2. Partnerships: If you have time but no money, find a partner with money but no time. You manage the rehab/tenants; they put up the $100k. Split equity.
  3. Turnkey vs. BRRRR: Turnkey requires more cash upfront. BRRRR (Fixer Upper) requires less down but more renovation cash. The total capital needed is often similar, just spent differently.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use a HELOC for the down payment?

Yes, but it adds risk. Now you have two payments (HELOC + New Mortgage). Ensure the rental income covers BOTH, or you are cash flow negative.

What about closing costs?

They are higher for investors. Budget 3-5%. You can sometimes ask the seller to cover these, but in a hot market, cash is expected.

Should I buy a REIT instead?

If you have <$50k, yes. Buying VNQ (Vanguard Real Estate ETF) gives you exposure to real estate without the massive capital requirement or the toilet repairs.
